Status of the unrestricted problem

Write m=d+1 and normalize the roots:

V=1⊥⊂Rm,uij​:=2​ei​−ej​​∈S(V),0≤i<j≤d.

This normalization is necessary because f is defined on the unit sphere.

The assertion for arbitrary odd f is a known open problem: it is the function-theoretic formulation of Makeev’s conjecture for the dual difference body of a regular simplex. Kuperberg proved the equivalence with the constant-width-body problem and proved the result in dimension 3. He also showed that the Euler-class obstruction used in dimension 3 vanishes in every dimension d≥4. NYJM+2NYJM+2

The Handbook of Discrete and Computational Geometry continues to state the odd-function formulation as a conjecture and notes that the corresponding homological count is even—and the primary equivariant obstruction disappears—for d≥4. A later monograph on constant-width bodies likewise reports confirmation only in dimension 3. I found no subsequent published resolution through July 2026. California State University, Northridge+1

Consequently, a complete proof for all smooth odd functions in even the first case d=4 would settle an open conjecture. What follows are several completely proved positive results, valid for every d, including a fairly large class of non-zonal functions and a C0-open set of arbitrary odd functions.

1. The test-map reduction

Let E be the vector space of antisymmetric edge-labels

y=(yij​)0≤i,j≤d​,yji​=−yij​,yii​=0.

Thus dimE=(2m​).

For c=(c0​,…,cd​)∈V, define

(δc)ij​:=2​ci​−cj​​.

These are precisely the restrictions of linear functions to the roots.

Lemma 1 — Exact edge labels

For y∈E, the following are equivalent.

  1. There is c∈V such that

    yij​=2​ci​−cj​​for all i,j.

  2. Every triangle sum vanishes:

    yij​+yjk​+yki​=0for all distinct i,j,k.

  3. For every antisymmetric m×m matrix X satisfying

    X1=0,

    one has

    i<j∑​Xij​yij​=0.

Proof

The implication 1⇒2 follows by telescoping.

Conversely, assume 2. Set c0​=0 and

ci​:=2​yi0​.

The triangle relation for (i,j,0) gives

yij​+yj0​+y0i​=0,

hence

yij​=yi0​−yj0​=2​ci​−cj​​.

Subtracting the mean of the ci​'s does not change their differences and places c in V.

To prove the equivalence with 3, observe that

i<j∑​Xij​(ci​−cj​)​=i∑​ci​j∑​Xij​.​

Thus every matrix X with X1=0 is orthogonal to every exact edge-label. Conversely, the exact edge-label space has dimension m−1=d, while

C:={X:XT=−X, X1=0}

has dimension

(2m​)−(m−1)=(2d​).

Hence C is exactly the orthogonal complement of the exact-label space. ∎

The space C is naturally the Lie algebra so(V): extend a skew operator on V by zero on R1.

For an odd continuous f, define

yf(A)ij​:=f(Auij​),A∈SO(V),

and let

Tf​(A):=projC​yf(A)∈C.

Corollary 2 — Test-map formulation

The desired conclusion holds for f if and only if

Tf​(A)=0

for some A∈SO(V).

Proof

If Tf​(A)=0, Lemma 1 gives c∈V such that

f(Auij​)=c⋅uij​.

Taking b=Ac gives

c⋅uij​=Ac⋅Auij​=b⋅Auij​.

The converse is immediate. ∎

Notice the dimension equality

dimSO(d)=(2d​)=dimC.

This is the source of the degree/Euler-class approach.

Under the rotation group of the Ad​ root system, Tf​ becomes a section of a rank-(2d​) bundle over a finite quotient of SO(d). The target representation is the adjoint representation twisted by the character recording global root inversion. Since the adjoint factor extends to SO(d), this bundle is a direct sum of copies of a line bundle. Kuperberg’s calculation shows that its Euler class is nonzero for d=3 but vanishes for d≥4. This explains precisely why the known topological proof stops at dimension 3; it neither proves nor disproves the assertion in higher dimensions. NYJM+2NYJM+2

2. A complete theorem for every odd cubic

The following result holds in every dimension, including all d>3.

Theorem 3 — Odd polynomials of degree at most three

Let d≥2. Suppose

f(x)=P(x)+ℓ(x),x∈S(V),

where P is an arbitrary homogeneous cubic polynomial on V and ℓ is linear. Then there exist A∈SO(V) and b∈V such that

f(Auij​)=b⋅Auij​for every i<j.

Equivalently, the conjecture holds for every odd function whose spherical-harmonic expansion has only degrees 1 and 3.

Proof

Define the distinguished cubic

p(x):=i=0∑d​xi3​,x=(x0​,…,xd​)∈V.

We first establish a tensor identity.

Every cubic Q on V has a unique symmetric trilinear polarization TQ​ satisfying

Q(x)=TQ​(x,x,x).

Extend TQ​ to Rm by projecting each argument orthogonally onto V. Write

(TQ​)abc​:=TQ​(ea​,eb​,ec​).

Equip the space of cubics with the SO(V)-invariant tensor inner product

⟨Q,R⟩:=a,b,c=0∑d​(TQ​)abc​(TR​)abc​.

Let SO(V) act on cubics by

(g⋅Q)(x):=Q(g−1x).

For X∈so(V), the infinitesimal action on p is

(X⋅p)(x)​=dtd​​t=0​p(e−tXx)=−3i,j∑​Xij​xi2​xj​.​

Consequently,

⟨Q,X⋅p⟩=−3i,j∑​Xij​(TQ​)iij​.(2.1)

On the other hand,

Q(ei​−ej​)=(TQ​)iii​−3(TQ​)iij​+3(TQ​)ijj​−(TQ​)jjj​.

Therefore

i<j∑​Xij​Q(ei​−ej​)​=21​i,j∑​Xij​((TQ​)iii​−3(TQ​)iij​+3(TQ​)ijj​−(TQ​)jjj​).​

The terms containing (TQ​)iii​ and (TQ​)jjj​ vanish because X1=0. Moreover,

i,j∑​Xij​(TQ​)ijj​=−i,j∑​Xij​(TQ​)iij​,

by interchanging i and j, using Xji​=−Xij​ and the symmetry of TQ​. Hence

i<j∑​Xij​Q(ei​−ej​)=−3i,j∑​Xij​(TQ​)iij​.

Together with (2.1), this gives the central identity

⟨Q,X⋅p⟩=i<j∑​Xij​Q(ei​−ej​)=22​i<j∑​Xij​Q(uij​).​(2.2)

Now consider the continuous function

Ψ:SO(V)⟶R,Ψ(A):=⟨P,A⋅p⟩.

Since SO(V) is compact, Ψ has a maximum at some A0​.

For every X∈so(V),

0​=dtd​​t=0​Ψ(A0​etX)=⟨P,A0​⋅(X⋅p)⟩=⟨A0−1​⋅P,X⋅p⟩,​

where the last equality uses invariance of the tensor inner product.

Put

Q:=A0−1​⋅P.

With our action convention,

Q(x)=P(A0​x).

By (2.2),

i<j∑​Xij​P(A0​uij​)=0for every X∈C.

Lemma 1 therefore gives c∈V such that

P(A0​uij​)=2​ci​−cj​​=c⋅uij​.

Thus, with bP​=A0​c,

P(A0​uij​)=bP​⋅A0​uij​.

Finally, write ℓ(x)=a⋅x, a∈V. Then

ℓ(A0​uij​)=a⋅A0​uij​.

Taking

b:=A0​c+a

gives

b⋅A0​uij​​=c⋅uij​+a⋅A0​uij​=P(A0​uij​)+ℓ(A0​uij​)=f(A0​uij​),​

as required. ∎

Remark

This proof is genuinely dimension-independent. The key fact is the exact variational identity (2.2): the cycle defect of a cubic is the derivative of its correlation with the symmetric cubic p=∑xi3​.

3. An open set of arbitrary odd functions

The cubic theorem is stable: the property is not confined to polynomials.

Theorem 4 — Uniform stability near ∑xi3​

For every d≥2, there exists εd​>0 such that every continuous odd

f:S(V)→R

satisfying

∥f−p∥∞​<εd​,p(x)=i=0∑d​xi3​,

has the required rotation A and linear function b.

The same conclusion holds in a neighborhood of every nonzero scalar multiple or rotation of p, and adding an arbitrary linear function does not affect the assertion.

Proof

For f∈Codd​(S(V)), let

Tf​(A)=projC​(f(Auij​))i<j​.

Since

p(uij​)=(2​1​)3+(−2​1​)3=0,

we have

Tp​(I)=0.

We calculate the derivative at I. Let X∈so(V)=C. For u=uij​,

dpu​(Xu)=3k∑​uk2​(Xu)k​=23​((Xu)i​+(Xu)j​).

Now

(Xu)i​=−2​Xij​​,(Xu)j​=−2​Xij​​.

Consequently,

dpuij​​(Xuij​)=−2​3​Xij​.

The resulting edge-label already belongs to C, so

DTp​(I)[X]=−2​3​X.(3.1)

In particular, DTp​(I) is an isomorphism.

Choose a sufficiently small ball B about 0 in so(V) such that the exponential map is injective on B and the map

Fp​(X):=Tp​(eX)

has no zero on ∂B. By (3.1), its local Brouwer degree at 0 is

deg(Fp​,B,0)=sgndet(−2​3​I)=0.

Let

η:=X∈∂Bmin​∥Fp​(X)∥>0.

If N=(2d+1​), then for every A,

∥Tf​(A)−Tp​(A)∥​≤(i<j∑​∣f(Auij​)−p(Auij​)∣2)1/2≤N​∥f−p∥∞​.​

Choose

εd​<2N​η​.

For the straight-line homotopy

ft​=p+t(f−p),0≤t≤1,

the maps Fft​​ remain nonzero on ∂B. Homotopy invariance of Brouwer degree gives

deg(Ff​,B,0)=deg(Fp​,B,0)=0.

The existence property of the Brouwer degree therefore yields X∈B with

Ff​(X)=0.

Taking A=eX and applying Lemma 1 gives the required b. ∎

Thus, in every dimension d>3, the set of odd functions satisfying the conclusion contains a nonempty open subset of the entire Banach space Codd​(Sd−1).

4. All zonal odd functions

There is another infinite-dimensional class for which the conjecture holds.

Theorem 5 — Zonal functions

Let d≥2, let a∈S(V), and let h:[−1,1]→R be continuous and odd. Then every function

f(x)=h(a⋅x)+ℓ(x),

where ℓ is linear, satisfies the conclusion.

Proof

It is enough to treat ℓ=0, since a linear summand can simply be added to b.

Choose any nontrivial partition

{0,…,d}=S⊔T.

Let s=∣S∣, t=∣T∣, so s+t=m. Define c∈V by

ci​=⎩⎨⎧​α:=smt​​,β:=−tms​​,​i∈S,i∈T.​

Then

i∑​ci​=0,∥c∥=1.

Since SO(V) acts transitively on S(V), choose A∈SO(V) such that

ATa=c.

Therefore

a⋅Auij​=c⋅uij​=2​ci​−cj​​.

Put

κ:=2​α−β​>0.

The quantity a⋅Auij​ is:

  • 0 if i,j lie in the same part;

  • κ if i∈S,j∈T;

  • −κ if i∈T,j∈S.

Since h is odd,

f(Auij​)=⎩⎨⎧​0,h(κ),−h(κ),​i,j in the same part,i∈S,j∈T,i∈T,j∈S.​

Define z∈Rm by

zi​={2​h(κ),0,​i∈S,i∈T.​

After subtracting its mean, we may assume z∈V, without changing any difference zi​−zj​. Then

f(Auij​)=2​zi​−zj​​=z⋅uij​.

Taking b=Az proves

f(Auij​)=b⋅Auij​.

∎

Conclusion

The unrestricted assertion for every smooth odd f remains open for every d>3; in particular, there is no currently verified complete proof for d=4. The primary Euler-class method is known to fail there, but its failure does not produce a counterexample because arbitrary nowhere-zero sections of the test bundle need not arise from evaluating one scalar function on rotated roots. NYJM+1

The complete results proved above are:

The assertion holds in every dimension for all odd cubics plus linear functions.​ It holds on a nonempty C0-open set of arbitrary odd functions in every dimension.​ It holds for every continuous zonal odd function, with an arbitrary linear summand.​

The cubic theorem is particularly broad: it covers the full Sym3(V∗) representation, not merely symmetric or one-variable examples, and its proof uses a dimension-independent variational normal-form argument.
